clinicalPearls: Nocardiosis is usually an opportunistic infection occurring primarily in hosts with impaired defenses, especially defects in cell-mediated immunity and specific phagocyte function; typical risk factors include solid organ or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, systemic corticosteroids or Cushing syndrome, other immunosuppressive therapy, and HIV infection (p.1358-1359).

Pulmonary disease is the usual portal after inhalation of fragmented mycelia; onset is typically subacute over days to weeks (more acute in the severely immunocompromised), with prominent cough producing thick non-malodorous purulent sputum, fever, anorexia, and malaise (p.1359).

Typical chest imaging shows infiltrates, nodules, and masses in one or more lobes, and nodules frequently cavitate; pleural effusion or empyema occurs in about one-third of cases, occasionally without lung involvement (p.1359).
Dissemination occurs in up to one-third of patients with pneumonia, most often to the CNS and to skin/subcutaneous tissues; virtually any organ can be involved (p.1359-1360).

CNS involvement occurs in up to two-thirds of disseminated cases; brain imaging classically shows one or more ring-enhancing, multilobulated lesions, and multiple abscesses are seen in two-thirds of patients (p.1360).

Diagnosis starts with examining sputum or pus for branching, beaded, Gram-positive filaments (~1 um wide, up to 50 um long) that fragment into apparent cocci/coccobacilli; most nocardiae are modified (weak) acid-fast (e.g., modified Kinyoun, modified Ziehl-Neelsen, Fite-Faraco) (p.1360-1361).

Primary cutaneous nocardiosis follows transcutaneous inoculation (often thorn/gardening injury) and takes three forms: cellulitis, lymphocutaneous (sporotrichoid) syndrome, or actinomycetoma; N. brasiliensis is the usual cause of skin-limited and lymphocutaneous disease and of actinomycetoma (p.1358, p.1360).

Nocardiosis tends to remit and relapse; without definitive treatment, pulmonary disease characteristically follows a course of remissions and exacerbations over weeks to months, and prolonged therapy (months) is required (p.1359, p.1362-Table 179-1).
harrison.pathophysiology: Nocardia species are saprophytic, filamentous, aerobic Gram-positive bacteria ubiquitous in soil, water, and decaying organic matter; their cell walls contain mycolic acids and trehalose (Mycobacteriales order), and they are weakly (modified) acid-fast and catalase positive. Pulmonary and systemic disease follow inhalation of fragmented bacterial mycelia, while primary cutaneous and ocular disease follow direct inoculation. Most immunocompetent people clear inhaled nocardiae without disease; invasive infection is favored by impaired host defenses. Innate and adaptive responses, with neutrophils and macrophages central to antinocardial defense (underscored by the frequency of nocardiosis in chronic granulomatous disease), normally control the organism. Nocardiae have evolved mechanisms to survive within phagocytes, including neutralization of oxidants and prevention of phagosome-lysosome fusion and phagosome acidification; neutrophils limit but do not efficiently kill them. The characteristic pathology is an abscess with neutrophilic infiltration and prominent necrosis, with little fibrosis/encapsulation, whereas actinomycetoma shows granulomatous inflammation with sinus tract formation. (p.1358-1359)
additionalDifferentials: Lymphocutaneous (sporotrichoid) presentation overlaps with Sporothrix schenckii and Mycobacterium marinum infection (p.1360).

Mycetoma differential: actinomycetoma (filamentous bacteria, e.g., Nocardia), eumycetoma (fungal), and botryomycosis (cocci/bacilli, often Staphylococcus aureus) are difficult to separate clinically and require granule microscopy, culture, or biopsy (p.1361).
Ocular nocardiosis (keratitis, scleritis, endophthalmitis) cannot be distinguished from other ocular infections by signs and symptoms alone (p.1360).
infectionMimics: Other causes of pulmonary nodules/cavitation and ring-enhancing brain lesions in immunocompromised hosts (e.g., fungi, mycobacteria, toxoplasmosis as discussed in brain abscess context)
nonInfectiousMimics: Pulmonary or cerebral malignancy/metastases presenting as nodules, masses, or ring-enhancing lesions
additionalInvestigations: Sputum or pus microscopy for branching beaded Gram-positive filaments plus modified (weak-acid) acid-fast staining; organisms may also take up silver stains (p.1360-1361).
Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid or lung biopsy when sputum smears are negative, as they frequently are in pulmonary nocardiosis (p.1361).

Selective media (colistin-nalidixic acid agar, modified Thayer-Martin agar, or buffered charcoal-yeast extract agar) for mixed-flora specimens; avoid mycobacterial decontamination procedures, which can kill nocardiae; alert the laboratory to incubate cultures for prolonged periods (up to 2-4 weeks) (p.1361).

Species/complex identification by MALDI-TOF or genomic sequencing (16S rRNA, secA1, hsp65, or gyrB), with antimicrobial susceptibility testing (ideally CLSI broth dilution); susceptibility testing requires experience because nocardiae grow slowly and clump (p.1361).
Granule examination in mycetoma: wash suspect particles in saline, examine microscopically, and culture; culture is the most reliable way to identify the causative organism (p.1361).
Contrast-enhanced CNS imaging (MRI preferred, with IV gadolinium more sensitive than CT) in all patients with non-cutaneous/non-ocular nocardiosis to detect occult brain abscess (p.1360-1362).

Testing for underlying immunodeficiency in patients lacking typical risk factors, including HIV testing; test for chronic granulomatous disease in children and adults with nocardiosis who have no major risk factor (p.1359, p.1362).
redFlags: CNS dissemination: brain abscess may be clinically silent, so absence of neurologic symptoms does not exclude it - one-third of patients with CNS involvement have no CNS symptoms and one-fourth have no apparent pulmonary disease at presentation (p.1360).
Disseminated nocardiosis carries a higher mortality than localized pulmonary disease, especially with CNS involvement (p.1362).
Nocardiosis in a patient without a major risk factor should prompt evaluation for an undiagnosed immunologic defect, including HIV and chronic granulomatous disease (p.1359, p.1362).
harrison.prognosis: With appropriate treatment, mortality for localized pulmonary nocardiosis is less than 10%. Disseminated disease carries a higher mortality, especially with CNS involvement. Primary cutaneous and ocular disease often respond to therapy. Mortality from actinomycetoma is exceedingly low, but patients often suffer substantial morbidity, disfigurement, disability, and/or stigmatization. Prolonged therapy is required and disease tends to relapse, so secondary prophylaxis is considered by some experts for patients who remain at high risk after completing antimicrobial therapy. (p.1362)
pitfalls: Failing to image the brain: because brain abscess may be asymptomatic, all patients with pulmonary or systemic nocardiosis should have contrast-enhanced CNS imaging (MRI preferred) regardless of neurologic symptoms (p.1360, p.1362).

Missing the diagnosis on smear: sputum smears are frequently negative in pulmonary nocardiosis, and the modified (weak) acid-fast technique must be used or organisms may be overlooked; standard mycobacterial decontamination can kill nocardiae (p.1360-1361).

Cultures lost to short incubation: nocardiae grow slowly (colonies up to 2 weeks, characteristic appearance up to 4 weeks), so the laboratory must be informed to incubate cultures for prolonged periods (p.1361).

Overcalling colonization or contamination: Nocardia can colonize the respiratory tract in bronchiectasis/structural lung disease, and isolation from a respiratory specimen does not always indicate infection; blood culture isolates may be contaminants in low-risk patients without clinical disease (p.1361).
Adjunctive topical corticosteroids should NOT be given to patients with nocardial keratitis (p.1362).
harrison.severityClassification: Disease is categorized clinically and by host status to guide therapy duration: pulmonary/systemic disease in hosts with intact defenses versus deficient defenses, CNS disease, primary cutaneous disease (cellulitis, lymphocutaneous), osteomyelitis/arthritis/laryngitis/sinusitis, actinomycetoma, and keratitis - longer courses for immunocompromised and CNS disease, with indefinite therapy considered in some AIDS patients with CD4 below 200/uL or chronic granulomatous disease (p.1362). [Durations noted as classification context only; not dosing guidance.]
management: Begin antimicrobial therapy with a sulfonamide, co-trimoxazole (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) being the mainstay agent
Use combination therapy for severe, disseminated or central nervous system disease, adding a carbapenem such as imipenem with amikacin, or ceftriaxone or linezolid
Tailor the regimen to species identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing given variable resistance across Nocardia species
Treat for a prolonged course of many months, extending duration for cerebral or immunocompromised disease, with secondary prophylaxis where immunosuppression persists
Drain or resect abscesses and empyema surgically, including cerebral abscesses that fail to respond
Reduce immunosuppression where feasible in transplant and steroid-treated patients
Image the brain to detect occult abscess and monitor the response to treatment for relapse
Manage through an infectious diseases service
